Detecting departure and destination aerodromes from ADS-B

Version 5.1 — why arrivals are hard, and what recovers part of them

Author

EUROCONTROL Performance Review Unit

Published

August 10, 2026

Summary

Version 4 established that arrivals are harder than departures on every measure and recommended not changing the arrivals algorithm. It did not say why, and “we do not know why” is a poor basis for leaving a quarter of the data unlabelled. This version takes the arrival deficit apart.

Three findings.

The arrival deficit is silence, not error. Of 87,152 in-area arrivals, 3,011 are answered wrongly and 21,009 are not answered at all. Version 4’s emphasis on misnaming — built on a vivid case, Bilbao — described 12.54% of the problem.

Most of that silence is ours, but it is not cheap to break. 13,300 flights had a usable candidate that the abstention refused; only 7,709 had nothing at all. So the recoverable share is nearly twice the permanently lost one. But guessing on the refused flights scores 28.27% — four right for eleven wrong. The abstention is doing its job.

One new signal beats that, and it is horizontal. Whether the aircraft’s course points at the candidate aerodrome, measured tightly enough, recovers 425 correct arrivals for only 97 new errors — 4.38:1, past the 2:1 exchange rate version 4.5 argued for, and the first thing tested to clear it. Vertical rate recovers nothing, and adding it destroys most of the gain.

It is still not adoptable, for a reason outside its own comparison. The bearing test improves endpoint; production runs trend on arrivals, and trend beats the improved endpoint on both axes. The signal is real and the rule it improves is the wrong one (Section 7).

There is a single reason for that asymmetry, and it is the most useful thing in this paper:

ImportantPositions survive staleness; rates do not

The OpenSky archive fills every second by carrying the last known position forward, and in this population roughly half the rows are repeats. A bearing between two genuinely measured fixes is correct regardless of when they were measured. A rate divides by an elapsed time the timestamps get wrong — the clock says ten minutes, the two real measurements may be ninety seconds apart.

That one sentence explains why bearing alignment works, and why vertical rate, closing rate and the approach cone of version 4.5 all failed.

Two thirds of the deficit is at large airports and a quarter is out-of-area. This paper addresses the first; the second remains the largest untouched block and is left for a successor.

2 Silence, not error

“Not labelled” hides two situations that need opposite responses: no candidate existed, which is a receiver-coverage fact, and a candidate existed and the rule refused it, which is a choice. nearest never abstains, so its coverage is exactly the rate at which a candidate existed — no new computation is needed to separate them.

The 87,152 in-area arrivals, decomposed. In-area means the true destination is a real aerodrome, so out-of-area flights are excluded.
Outcome Flights Share
correctly labelled 63,132 72.44%
answered, wrong 3,011 3.45%
candidate existed, abstained 13,300 15.26%
no candidate anywhere 7,709 8.85%

8.85% of in-area arrivals have no candidate at all. That is the hard ceiling: no endpoint-based method can exceed 91.15% coverage on this data, whatever rule it uses.

3 The abstained block is hard, not neglected

The 13,300 refused flights look like free coverage. They are not.

endpoint answers a subset of what nearest answers, and on shared flights both rank candidates by the same effective distance, so they return identical answers there. nearest’s extra correct answers are therefore exactly its score on the refused block: 3,760 of 13,300, or 28.27%.

Answering them all would add 3,760 correct labels and 9,540 wrong ones — 0.39:1. Against the exchange rate version 4.5 argued for, that is not close. “Relax the thresholds for arrivals” is now priced, and the price is bad.

Why are they hard? Because of what an arrival endpoint is. The state-vector decimation study measured that an arrival’s last fix carries a position measured a median of 190 s earlier — at approach speed, roughly eight nautical miles back up the approach. The endpoint is not where the flight ended. Position alone cannot identify an aerodrome from eight miles out on a busy terminal area, and the abstention correctly declines to try.

4 Bearing alignment

If position is exhausted, motion might not be. The measure is the angle between the direction the aircraft actually travelled over a window and the direction of the candidate aerodrome, seen from the far end of that window. Zero degrees means the track runs straight at it.

This involves no extrapolated position — it is an angle between two observed bearings — so the documented failures of trajectory extrapolation in version 2 and the 2025 PRC report do not bind it.

NoteWhy departures need no 180-degree correction

A departing aircraft flies away from its aerodrome, so it looks as though the measure must be inverted for departures. It must not, because the origin of the angle already flips with the role.

The window is measured from the arrival’s last fix and the departure’s first, so its far end is earlier in time for an arrival and later for a departure. The bearing from that far end toward the near end is therefore the course in one case and the reverse course in the other. The question becomes “is the aerodrome in the direction I am heading” for an arrival and “is the aerodrome in the direction I came from” for a departure, and both read zero for a correct match.

The distinction matters because the two vertical and horizontal rates in the same analysis do carry an explicit per-role sign — they are signed along the time axis, and an angle between two bearings from a common origin is not. Confirmed empirically: correctly identified departures sit at a median of 2–9 degrees, not 171–178.

It also explains part of why the measure is weak for departures. By 30 minutes down-track the separation is 6 degrees against 2 — from far enough away, the true origin aerodrome and its neighbours all lie in much the same direction, so the angle stops discriminating. An arrival endpoint sits a median of eight nautical miles short of the runway, where the direction along the track is still informative.

Correct labels per error on the abstained arrival block, by window and angle gate. The block’s own baseline is 0.37. Note that these are computed on in-area truth only, and so overstate the population-level trade – see the next section.

Three things are visible and all three make physical sense.

Short windows carry no information. At 2–3 minutes every cell sits near the 0.37 baseline. Over two minutes the aircraft’s displacement is small against its position error, so the bearing is noise.

It switches on at 5 minutes and peaks at 7. A metric that were an artefact would not have an interior optimum with noise on both sides.

The gate should tighten as the window lengthens. At loose gates short windows win, because over half an hour everything points roughly everywhere. At 1° that reverses — a long baseline gives a more precise bearing, so a tight gate becomes meaningful rather than noise.

Accuracy plateaus at 70–76% however tight the gate. Roughly one arrival in four that points straight at an aerodrome lands somewhere else. Bearing alone has a ceiling, and tuning it further is close to exhausted.

Because the bearing test only ever adds answers — a flight that already passed the abstention is untouched, and the aerodrome named is the same candidate either way — every newly answered flight falls in exactly one of the two delta columns. Their sum is the number of flights the gate rescued, and

\[\text{accuracy on the rescued} = \frac{\Delta\text{correct}}{\Delta\text{correct} + \Delta\text{wrong}}\]

is how often the gate is right when it overrides the abstention. It is not the model’s accuracy, which is swamped by the flights the change never touched: at 3° the gate is right 63.67% of the time on the 1,503 flights it rescues, while the model’s accuracy reads 94.92%. The benchmark to hold it against is 28.27% — what guessing blind on that population scores (Section 3).

The gate must be tight, and tighter than seems physical. The ratio climbs monotonically as the gate narrows — 1.75:1 at 3°, 2.14:1 at 1°, 4.38:1 at 0.1° — and accuracy on the rescued flights rises with it, from 63.67% to 81.42%. Under 2:1 pricing the best gate is the tightest tested.

NoteA prediction this refuted

Before running the sub-degree gates we argued they could not help. A runway complex spans 2–4 km, which from 40 NM subtends 2–3°, so a gate below a degree is tighter than the target: it should stop selecting for “heading to this airport” and start selecting for “aimed at the arbitrary reference coordinate OurAirports publishes”. Accuracy was predicted to plateau and counts to collapse into noise.

Accuracy did not plateau. It rose from 63.67% at 3° to 81.42% at 0.1°, monotonically, on 522 flights — not a handful.

The reasoning was wrong about what the gate selects. It is not resolving which runway an aircraft is aimed at; it is separating tracks deliberately pointed at a field, over a long straight leg, from tracks that happen to line up by coincidence. Coincidental alignment is common at 3° and rare at 0.1°, and that is the whole of the discrimination.

Volume and rate trade against each other, and the rate wins. The widest gate tested, +bearing 30 min / 1 deg, recovers 2,295 correct labels — five times the tightest — but at 1.49:1 it costs 779 on the 2:1 reckoning. Chasing volume here is what the exchange rate exists to prevent.

Departures lose. The same test adds 8 correct departures for 89 errors, 0.09:1. Consistent with everything this study has found: departures are not short of evidence, and adding evidence to a rule that is not short of it costs accuracy. Bearing should not be applied to departures.

WarningThe block-level ratios were optimistic, and this is why

The abstained-block sweep reports 2.52:1 at 7 min / 3°. The same rule on the full population gives 1.75:1 — the same gate, the same rule, a third less. The difference is entirely the out-of-area flights the block analysis filtered out and the population cannot.

The lesson generalises: a rule evaluated on the subset it was designed for will beat its own field performance, and by a wide margin. Every ratio quoted in Section 4 should be read as an upper bound.

6 Why the vertical channel is dead

Vertical rate is the obvious second signal, and it does not work. Two independent measures of the same quantity — the broadcast vert_rate, and an ordinary least squares fit of altitude on time across the window — agree in sign at close to chance.

Sign agreement between vertical measures on the abstained arrival block. 50% is chance.
Window vert_rate vs OLS 2-point vs OLS rows with vert_rate = 0 rows fresher than 5 s
5 min 43.04% 47.13% 44.85% 10.58%
10 min 51.88% 59.80% 45.29% 28.87%
20 min 57.56% 64.28% 46.70% 43.92%
The same agreement at 20 minutes, banded by the share of rows carrying a position fresher than 5 s. Agreement tracks freshness, which identifies the cause rather than inferring it.
Window freshness Flights vert_rate vs OLS 2-point vs OLS
<30% fresh 11,960 49.76% 55.39%
30-60% 10,451 59.71% 60.43%
60-90% 11,309 62.50% 77.51%
>=90% fresh 1,067 71.79% 61.39%

Agreement rises with freshness, and 44.85% of rows carry a vertical rate of exactly zero — the signature of a value held over rather than measured. There is no vertical signal to extract here in either form.

The measured consequence is in the comparison table: adding the vertical test to the bearing test cuts the arrival gain from 425 correct to 102, and the ratio from 4.38:1 to 0.60:1. It does not merely fail to help — it discards flights the bearing test correctly rescued.

7 Recommendation

ImportantThe bearing test improves endpoint, and endpoint is still the wrong rule for arrivals

The comparison above scores every variant against the endpoint base. Scored against production instead, the picture changes completely.

Arrivals against production. The best bearing variant still loses on both axes.
Model Coverage Accuracy Overall Correct Wrong
trend (production) 68.06% 97.87% 66.61% 63,361 1,377
endpoint 30 NM / 15,000 ft 69.10% 95.63% 66.08% 62,856 2,870
endpoint + bearing 0.10 deg 69.66% 95.52% 66.54% 63,292 2,967

trend returns 69 more correct arrivals and 1,590 fewer wrong ones. It dominates: there is no exchange rate at which the bearing model wins.

The bearing test is a real signal and it genuinely improves endpoint. But endpoint was never the right rule for arrivals — version 4.5 concluded that already — so improving it does not produce a rule worth adopting. Earlier drafts of this section recommended the bearing test for arrivals without checking it against production. That was an error of comparison, not of measurement.

Departures: endpoint at 30 NM, 15,000 ft, 10 NM scheduled-service penalty. Against production this is +10,993 correct labels for +645 wrong, about 17:1. Unchanged from version 4.5 and still the one clear win in this study.

Arrivals: keep trend. Nothing in versions 4, 5 or 5.1 beats it.

Do not apply the bearing test to departures — every gate is a loss, the best at 0.55:1. Do not pursue vertical rate (Section 6). Do not use bearing as a veto, a replacement or a naming rule (Section 8).

Publish the provenance columns. adep_source / ades_source distinguish “named an aerodrome”, “outside the observed area” and “could not determine”, which are one indistinguishable null in the published flight list today. Still the highest value per line of code in the study.

7.1 What the bearing test still needs

It has only ever been tested as a rescue for endpoint’s abstention. trend — the rule actually recommended for arrivals — abstains on about a third of them, and whether bearing can rescue those flights is untested. That is the experiment that would give this finding somewhere to land, and the machinery now exists to run it.

And out-of-area remains the larger prize: 24.53% of the arrival deficit, 7,809 flights, current recall 1.95%. Unlike the abstained block, nobody has shown it is hard.

8 Bearing on the whole sample

Used as a rescue, the bearing test can only add answers. That is a structural limit rather than a property of the data: a flight the abstention already accepts is untouched, so the 2,870 arrivals the base rule gets wrong were unreachable by every variant in Section 5. No rescue can raise accuracy.

Applying the test to every flight opens three questions the rescue framing cannot ask.

  • Veto — require alignment on flights the gate accepts, so bearing can remove answers. The only variant that can raise accuracy.
  • Replace — alignment instead of the distance and height gate, testing whether that box carries anything the course does not.
  • Rerank — choose which aerodrome by alignment rather than by effective distance. Version 4.5 argued the abstention is a gate and never a naming rule, and that arrivals fail by misnaming; this is the naming rule that argument implies.
Arrivals: the bearing test used four ways. Only the rescue helps; the other three are catastrophic.
Model Coverage Accuracy Overall d correct d wrong

rescue: gate OR align<=0.1 69.66% 95.52% 66.54% 436 97
rescue: gate OR align<=3.0 70.75% 94.93% 67.16% 1,020 544

All three fail, and not marginally. The veto costs 41,585 correct arrivals at 3°. Replace costs 40,565. Rerank costs 33,396 correct labels and adds 1,729 wrong ones, dropping accuracy from 95.63% to 86.50%.

8.1 Why: the measure is out of domain on flights that landed

The diagnosis is not that alignment is a weak signal. It is that the flights the gate already accepts are the wrong population to ask.

no course computable median alignment within 3° on ground at the endpoint
gate accepts 23.8% 21° 18.4% 43.1%
gate refuses 24.3% 53° 5.2% 0.6%

43% of accepted arrivals are on the ground at their endpoint. For those, the last seven minutes are the approach, the landing roll and the taxi to stand — and the “course” over that window is dominated by ground manoeuvring, which points wherever the taxiways happen to run. A further quarter have no computable course at all. A veto at 3° therefore rejects roughly four in five flights it should keep.

The bearing test was developed on the abstained block, where every endpoint is airborne and en route by construction. Its domain is airborne endpoints, and the flights the gate accepts are mostly not that. Used as a rescue it never leaves its domain, which is why it works there and nowhere else.

8.2 Rerank refutes the naming-rule argument

The reranking result deserves its own note, because version 4.5 predicted the opposite. Its argument was that the abstention decides only whether to answer and never what to answer, that arrivals fail predominantly by misnaming, and that a trajectory-based naming rule was therefore the most promising fix available.

Ranking candidates by alignment instead of distance is that rule, and it is far worse than ranking by distance. The reason is geometric: an aerodrome 200 NM directly ahead is perfectly aligned. Alignment has no sense of scale, so as a ranking criterion it systematically prefers distant aerodromes that happen to lie on the track. Distance was doing enormous work that the argument did not credit.

Alignment is a filter over distance-ranked candidates, not a ranking criterion. That is what the rescue variant does, and it is the only form in which the signal is worth anything.

NoteA small correction to Section 5

The whole-sample run computes alignment without requiring an altitude, because alignment is purely horizontal; Section 5’s figures came from a routine that also fitted the vertical slope and so discarded samples with no altitude. The rescue numbers here are consequently a little higher — 436 correct against 425 at the same gate. The direction and the recommendation are unchanged; the earlier figures were conservative.

9 What is now ruled out

Recorded so it is not re-attempted:

  • Relaxing the abstention thresholds — priced at 0.39:1 (Section 3).
  • The approach cone — version 4.5 measured it against the rectangle at matched coverage; departures lost up to 2.55 pp of accuracy, arrivals were a wash.
  • Bucket decimation — the state-vector study measured +55 correct arrivals per day for a change that rewrites track_id for every published row.
  • Vertical rate, in any form (Section 6).
  • Trajectory extrapolation — version 2 and the 2025 PRC report, independently.
  • Bearing as a veto, a replacement, or a naming rule (Section 8). Only the rescue form works, and only because it stays inside the measure’s domain.

10 Limitations

  • One sample. Three days, 2025-06-05 to 07. The operating points were chosen as the argmax over 120 grid cells of that same sample, so the ratios are optimistic. The 2° and 3° columns peak cleanly at 7 minutes, which is why the region is credible; the specific numbers are not validated.
  • Two measurement bugs were found in this work, both by sanity checks rather than by anything failing: angle_between used %, and Spark’s remainder keeps the sign of the dividend, so bearings 20° apart measured 340° whenever the pair straddled north — the tell was a median alignment of 186° on a 0–180° scale. And the altitude slope divided an altitude change by an elapsed time drawn from different rows, because min_by skips nulls where min does not. Both are fixed; both had already produced numbers that were reported before being caught.
  • The >=90% fresh band reverses the freshness trend for the 2-point measure, on about a thousand flights. Either small-sample noise or something real about very short tracks. Not resolved.
  • nearest and endpoint are assumed to answer identically where both answer, which underpins Section 3. It follows from both ranking on the same effective distance, but it is an argument, not a measurement.

python benchmarks/abstained_vertical.py --results-dir <dir>

# which vertical measure to trust, banded by freshness
python benchmarks/vertical_measure.py --results-dir <dir>

# base against the motion variants, whole population
